title: Will the iPad Ever Be a Worthy Mac Replacement?
body:
iOS 9 brought us multitasking on iPad. Here's how far we've come since.
            
                        
    
                    
        
        
        
    
                                Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                            
        
        
        September 10, 2026
            
            
                        Credit: David MAREUIL/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images/Lifehacker
                            
    
        
        Welcome to a new series called Apple a Day, where sites in the CNET family are sharing pieces of Apple content from our archives—an article, review and/or video—daily from now through late September. In addition to Lifehacker, this series will include pieces from our sibling sites PCMag, Mashable, CNET and Popular Science.For the first five years of its life, the iPad could only run one app at a time. Then, iOS 9 changed everything. That update, released 10 years ago this month, introduced multitasking to the Apple tablet for the first time. "Split View" let you run two apps side-by-side at once; "Slide Over" gave you quick access to a third app in an iPhone-style window; and Picture in Picture made it possible to watch a video while working on something else. In an article published at the time, these changes prompted Lifehacker to proclaim that "iOS 9 actually makes the iPad usable for work."In total, you could have up to four different windows on screen through this concoction of features, a huge improvement over the previous limit of "one." Coupled with the new keyboard shortcuts, iOS 9 transformed the iPad, and brought it closer to the laptop replacement so many users wanted it to be. "Closer" being the key word there. 
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
Multitasking on iPad is still a work in progressWhile iOS 9 made it possible to focus on more than one app at a time, it didn't address other iPad limitations that made it difficult for computer users to fully make the switch. In the 11 years since that update, Apple has chipped away at those issues slowly but surely, while upgrading the iPad's hardware exponentially. In iOS 11, Apple made it easier to launch an app into Split View from the Dock, and introduced cross-app drag and drop. With iPadOS 13, Apple introduced a desktop-class version of Safari, and rolled out the Files app, which even supported hard drives and SD cards. iPadOS 15 improved Split View and Slide Over accessibility, and made it possible to multitask with multiple windows from one app. By iPadOS 16, it seemed like Apple had had enough of people complaining that the iPad wasn't enough like a Mac. This update introduced Stage Manager, which let users display and resize multiple floating app windows on screen. You could even connect your compatible iPad to an external monitor to run Stage Manager on both displays, just as you might connect a MacBook to a monitor. iPadOS 17 improved the experience again, adding support for FaceTime calls from external webcams, while last year's iPadOS 26 provided another overhaul, introducing the closest thing to a macOS-like window system yet, right down to the traffic-light window buttons. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
We're at the point where, on the surface, the iPad can be considered Apple's answer to the touchscreen computer, especially when paired with a keyboard and trackpad. But in practical use, it's evident the iPad still isn't a Mac, even in cases where the iPad supports the apps and utilities you use on Mac. iPadOS doesn't feel designed for computer tasks; it feels like computer tasks were retrofitted to iPadOS. That doesn't mean things like multitasking and file support aren't welcome features, but the experience isn't as refined as it is on macOS. What's more, there is evidence Apple agrees the two devices are just too different, as rumors suggest the company might release a touchscreen MacBook as soon as next year. For me, iPadOS still feels at its best when I use one app at a time. All the above efforts to change its nature aside, that's probably because the iPad was originally designed that way. 
            
                        
                
            
                    
                                            
                
            
                Jake Peterson
                                    Senior Technology Editor
                                
                                            Covering tech news, how-to guides, explainers, and more.

title: Three Reasons You Shouldn't Use Your Browser's Password Manager (and What to Use Instead)
body:
Built-in tools have major limitations when it comes to security and functionality.
            
                        
    
                    
        
        
        
    
                                Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                            
        
        
        September 4, 2026
            
            
                        Credit:  Ian Moore/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
    
        
        Most modern browsers have built-in password management, allowing you to save your credentials and automatically fill them when logging into your accounts on various websites. And while Google Password Manager on Chrome and similar tools in other browsers like Firefox, Brave, and Microsoft Edge certainly simplify the process of storing and using stronger passwords, they have major limitations when it comes to security and functionality. Here's why you should use a dedicated password manager instead.Browser password managers only work within the browserIf you store your passwords in your browser, it can fill your credentials on websites within the browser itself. (If you're an Android user, Google Password Manager also syncs to your device and works across any browser or app.) But if you use multiple browsers or want to log into apps on your iPhone or PC, you'll have to manually copy and paste your password from the browser into those form fields—not ideal, from a standpoint of both convenience and security. Browser password managers are more vulnerable to security risksBrowser password management is, on a basic level, secure: Google uses the same AES encryption in transit and at rest that many dedicated password managers do, and allows it you to add biometric authentication for auto-filling credentials. However, they're not zero-knowledge by default: Google manages your encryption key unless you enable on-device encryption so that your vault can only be unlocked on your device, by you, with your Google password or biometrics. Firefox also uses AES-256 encryption and has a "primary password" feature to protect your stored data, without which anyone who has access to your computer or browser profile can view your saved passwords. It's on the user to add these layers of security, as they're not on by default.As Wired points out, the more serious problem isn't encryption, but rather the risk inherent in storing passwords in a high-value account that could be targeted—either by someone who gains access to your device or as part of a takeover attempt, such as a phishing or credential stuffing attack. This creates a single point of failure, and if someone gets into your Google account or your browser of choice, your passwords for everything else are also compromised. Browser password managers have only basic featuresBrowser password managers do basically one thing, which is store your login credentials and fill them in on websites when you visit them in the browser. Google Password Manager will also alert you if your password has been compromised in a breach, but most browsers lack any additional tools and features, such as password customization, secure sharing, email masking, emergency access, and storage for payment cards, identity data, and documents. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Use a dedicated third-party password manager insteadThe solution is to opt for a dedicated password manager that works across platforms and devices and offers a layer of protection outside of your browser. There are many excellent password managers to choose from, including free services like Bitwarden and privacy-focused Proton Pass (which also has a decent free tier). The best password managers also have features like secure file storage, encrypted credential sharing, and data breach monitoring, making them useful tools in your privacy and security arsenal. Of course, even a browser password manager is better than nothing at all, if the alternative is to reuse the same easy-to-remember credentials across your accounts. (It's also likely your reused passwords don't meet basic security standards and can be easily guessed.) Password storage in Chrome, Firefox, and other browsers do reduce the friction of shifting to strong, unique passwords for your accounts, and that alone is a solid step. But a third-party password manager is a superior choice if you're willing to invest a bit of time and energy into setting it up. 
            
                        
                
                    
                                            
                
                
                                            
    More by Emily

title: Apple's 'Reference Image' Preserves Your Original Photos (Even After You Edit Them)
description: Figuring out what’s real online is only getting harder, and AI watermarks can only go so far to identify fakes. But today, Apple int
body:
Figuring out what’s real online is only getting harder, and AI watermarks can only go so far to identify fakes. But today, Apple introduced a new standard to at least help identify real images taken directly on an iPhone: Apple Reference Image. It won’t solve the problem of finding the truth online, but it could be a helpful tool towards that goal.The new feature will be available on iPhone 18 Pro models to start. It works by taking signed sensor data from the camera and using it to create a reference picture that can’t be edited, alongside a version that can be changed. The idea here is to give you a version of the picture that’s authenticated at the moment of capture, which you can compare against any modified versions later.
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Credit: Apple
                    
    
This provenance metadata can be preserved through certain supported sharing methods, which for now means select other Apple devices can check their verification status. That doesn’t mean that anyone can check the veracity of an image—especially if the version that gets posted and shared is an edited variant—but it provides a tool for the person or organization that took the picture originally to offer proof of verification.
This tool comes alongside the announcement that Apple will soon add support for the SynthID standard. This will potentially help users identify when an image has been created or modified with AI. Apple joins a long (though not exactly comprehensive) list of major tech companies to support the standard, including OpenAI, Nvidia, and obviously Google, the original creator of SynthID.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
We’re still in the midst of a scattershot image verification ecosystem. Apple’s Reference Image is a clever implementation that gives the end user a signed original to compare a picture against, which is a step up from C2PA metadata that merely embeds information about an image’s origin. It’s still unclear how widely these verification tools will be implemented and how easy it will be for users to trace where an image comes from and how, precisely, it was modified, but still, something is better than nothing.

            ExperiencePradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

    Table of Contents
    
        
        The Linksys RE7000 Range Booster is designed to fill weak-signal gaps without changing your existing router, and it's currently on sale for just $27.99 as an open-box unit on StackSocial. Open box usually means the packaging has been handled or returned, but the unit itself has been checked and works like new. This model plugs straight into a wall outlet and keeps the top socket usable, so it doesn’t block access in tight spaces. In a typical home, Linksys claims coverage up to 2,500 square feet, though real-world results depend on walls and layout.Setup is simple: You press the WPS button to sync it with your router and use a phone or laptop to finish the process in a few minutes. It works with most routers, including those provided by internet service providers. Once it's in place, the extender works by pulling in your existing Wi-Fi signal and pushing it further into areas that struggle to stay connected. It supports AC1900 speeds across dual bands, which is enough for everyday use like streaming, browsing, or video calls, assuming your base connection is strong enough. MU-MIMO support helps when several people are connected at once, so one person streaming a show does not slow down someone else on a video call.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
There is also seamless roaming, which keeps your phone connected to the strongest signal automatically as you move around the house. The included Gigabit Ethernet port is also useful if you want a more stable wired connection for a console or desktop in a weak-signal area. That said, there are limits to what an extender like this can do—this is a Wi-Fi 5 extender, so it will not match the speeds or efficiency of newer Wi-Fi 6 or 7 hardware. But for $28, this Wi-Fi extender is a great deal for fixing dead zones in your house.

title: TikTok Just Announced These Four New Features for Comments
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 4, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: NurPhoto / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            TikTok announced four new features coming to its comment section over the next month.
                                            Next month, the app will roll out voice comments, which will let users record and post audio up to 60 seconds.
                                            Creators can add polls to their comment sections to invite viewers to vote on up to five options at a time.
                                            Finally, TikTok is rolling out photo carousel and Live Photos comments as well.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        TikTok is famous for its addictive algorithm. And while the videos are certainly the app's main focus, I find the most entertainment in the comments. TikTok commenters can be hilarious, especially since they can use both text and photos to make their jokes. Social media comments are often vile, and while TikTok isn't immune to trolls and their ilk, its comments are generally something else. Now, the comments are changing. On Thursday, TikTok announced four new features that will make comments more visual, interactive, and, well, loud. Not all of these features are out quite yet, but by next month, you might not recognize TikTok's comment section. Text and photo comments aren't going anywhere, but you may find that the comment section is about to get a bit louder. Starting next month, TikTok will support voice comments up to 60 seconds long, which adds a wholly unique type of comment to the mix. Based on TikTok's press release, you can still attach a text-based comment to your voice comment, similar to how photo comments work.While friends may post voice comments on each other's videos à la voice memos in a group chat, I'm guessing that commenters in general will use this feature in ways TikTok doesn't necessarily intend. In fact, this may birth a new type of meme, where users spam videos with obnoxious sound effects and reaction sounds. Think the sounds added to meme edits of viral videos, but in comment form. It's going to be messy, and, likely, hysterical.   
Starting this week, you may see a new interactive element to TikTok comments: polls. TikTok says creators can add polls to the comments of their videos, with up to five voting options per poll. Rather than ask for opinions in the comments, creators can use a poll instead. Creators can choose how long voting lasts, and watch votes appear in real time. It's a small change, but one that could be useful to both big and small creators looking for input from their viewers. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
You're no longer limited to posting static images in TikTok's comments. TikTok now supports uploading Live Photos to comments, which should also prove interesting. I could see people thinking they're posting a standard image, but accidentally uploading a Live Photo instead. But seeing as users already know how to add GIFs to comments, I'm not sure how many will want to upload Live Photos. This one might be reserved more for friends commenting on friends' videos, but we'll have to see how users react to know for sure. This last update is perhaps a bit more useful than Live Photo comments. TikTok says it's working on allowing users to upload up to nine photos in one comment, which means the comments section may be literally full of pictures once this launches en masse.  Like standard carousels, users will be able to swipe through your photo uploads, including in a full-screen view. This one will roll out over the course of this month.

title: A Bunch of AI Platforms Are Down, Including ChatGPT
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 3, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Robert Way via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok are all experiencing downtime Thursday morning.
                                            OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX AI all confirm issues with their platforms.
                                            It's not clear what the root cause of the issue is at this time, or whether the outages are related.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you had trouble accessing AI platforms Thursday morning, you're not alone. Apps and services, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok, were down, or experienced issues with service. ChatGPT and Grok were both unresponsive when I tried to use them, while Claude appeared to respond, at least for me. ChatGPT appears to be experiencing the most issues, at least per Downdetector. The site, which accepts user reports of issues with apps and services, currently shows tens of thousands of reports for ChatGPT alone. Claude and Grok had fewer reports, but still many (thousands) over the course of this morning. According to OpenAI's status page, the company had experienced issues with both ChatGPT and Codex. Anthropic had also acknowledged issues with Claude, including for its Mythos 5.1, Fable 5.1, and Opus 5 models, and said it is working on a fix. SpaceXAI shows that all Grok functions appear to be down at this time. As of 1:19 p.m. ET, all three services now report that they're now up and running. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
It's not clear exactly what caused these issues, or if they were all related to one another. Typically, outages like these are solved relatively quickly, so it's not a surprise that all three were able to get their systems back by early afternoon. I'll continue to monitor the situation and update this piece accordingly.

title: iPhones Are Getting More Expensive, but AirPods Are Cheaper Than Ever
body:
Khamosh Pathak
                            
        
            Khamosh Pathak
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceKhamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 9, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Apple
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple is increasing the price of all existing iPhone models, including iPhone 17e, iPhone 16, and iPhone 17.
                                            The newly released AirPods 5 are actually cheaper than the outgoing model.
                                            The Apple Watch series has surprisingly missed the price bump.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        RAMageddon is real, and it’s finally come for the iPhone. Thanks to the ever-increasing costs of memory and storage, the prices of virtually all tech products are going up. A couple of months ago, Apple increased the pricing for the Mac and the iPad, by a couple of hundred dollars. Now, it’s the iPhone’s turn: Suddenly, all the iPhones are now $100 more expensive than they were yesterday, and the newly announced models are $100 more expensive than last year. But it’s not all doom and gloom. The new AirPods are actually cheaper, and mercifully, some Apple products remain the same price.The $100 iPhone bump
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Khamosh Pathak
                    
    
At the September keynote event, Apple introduced the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 18 Pro Max. The 18 Pro starts at $1,199 for 256GB storage, and the iPhone 18 Pro Max is now $1,399. Both of them are $100 more than the starting price of comparable iPhone 17 Pro/Max models.
The price bump doesn't stop with the new phones: Apple has flipped a switch and bumped prices on all existing iPhone models by $100. While Apple did not introduce an iPhone 18, the price of the iPhone 17 has quietly gone up; it now starts at $899 for the 256GB model instead of $799. The older iPhone 16 model is now $799, while the "budget" iPhone 17e now sells for $699. Even the iPhone Air has gone up to $1099.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Apple Watch pricing stays the sameSurprisingly, the RAM and storage costs haven’t hit the Apple Watch yet, or, at least, Apple is willing to absorb those increases for these smaller devices. The Series 12 Apple Watch with a new S11 processor and on-device Apple Intelligence features starts at the same $399 price as the Apple Watch 11. The new Apple Watch Ultra 4 also remains at the same $799 introductory price as the Ultra 3.AirPods are now cheaper (and better) than everOne popular product escaped the price bump: I was surprised to see a new standard AirPods model at the iPhone 18 Pro keynote, but the price drop was even more unexpected. The base AirPods 5 now come with built-in ANC (which used to cost extra), along with better transparency and improved sound features, and they are just $129, the cost of the outgoing AirPods 4 without ANC. Apple does have a more expensive model of AirPods 5 that comes with a wireless charging case, better battery life, and an on-stem voice control feature for $149, or $30 cheaper than the outgoing AirPods 4 with ANC model.

title: Microsoft's Record-Setting Patch Tuesday Update Fixes Nearly 1,000 Flaws
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

        September 9, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Beata Zawrzel/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Microsoft just released fixes for nearly 1,000 bugs, which is approaching double the number of flaws patched in July.
                                            Two of the vulnerabilities addressed this month are zero-days that have been exploited in the wild.
                                            AI is making it easier for bad actors to develop tools to exploit vulnerabilities as well as allowing developers to fix them more quickly.
                                            It's always been important to install security updates as soon as they're available, but it's even more critical now with a larger number of flaws open to exploitation.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Security updates have been trending larger, and Microsoft's Patch Tuesday for September is no exception. The company just released fixes for nearly 1,000 bugs, which is approaching double the number of flaws patched in July (the previous record). Two of the vulnerabilities addressed this month are zero-days that have been exploited in the wild. This massive jump is in large part due to AI, which is making it easier for bad actors to develop tools to exploit vulnerabilities while also allowing developers to find and fix them more quickly. This means we're likely to continue seeing sizeable updates on shorter release cycles, ideally reducing the time hackers have to take advantage of these flaws. Microsoft has typically pushed Patch Tuesday fixes around 10 a.m. PT on the second Tuesday of every month. It's always been important to install security updates as soon as they're available, but it's even more critical now with a larger number of flaws open to exploitation. PC users should receive Patch Tuesday updates automatically, but you can check the status via Start > Settings > Windows Update > Check for Windows updates.
September's Patch Tuesday addresses 966 flaws with two zero-days As BleepingComputer reports, the 966 flaws fixed this month are broken down across the following categories: 438 elevation-of-privilege vulnerabilities, 19 security feature bypass vulnerabilities, 258 remote-code-execution vulnerabilities, 173 information disclosure vulnerabilities, 16 spoofing vulnerabilities, and 56 denial-of-service vulnerabilities. These figures do not include other vulnerabilities (204 in total across other Microsoft products) patched earlier this month. One of the zero-days addressed in September is an elevation of privilege vulnerability in the Windows Update Stack. CVE-2026-81963 allows attackers to gain SYSTEM privileges via improper link resolution before file access. The bug discovery has been attributed to Romain Deperne and the Microsoft Threat Intelligence Centre. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The other zero-day is also an elevation of privilege vulnerability. CVE-2026-85880 is a flaw in the Windows Advanced Local Procedure—an attacker could execute code in a low-privilege AppContainer, and the vulnerability could escape the sandbox and gain SYSTEM privileges locally. The bug was discovered by Volexity, as well as Mark Kelly, David Galazin, and Jeremy Hedges with Proofpoint. Both zero-days have been actively exploited in the wild, though Microsoft has not provided any details as to how.

        The original Nintendo Switch still has plenty of life left, and right now this refurbished bundle is on sale for just $189.99 on StackSocial. It includes the console, dock, red and blue Joy-Con controllers, and the cables needed to get started. This is the original 2017 model, not the OLED version, so the display and battery are a step behind newer revisions. Even so, it delivers the same core idea: you can take your games anywhere. Its 6.2-inch touchscreen is sharp enough for everyday play, and the system is small enough to toss into a bag without thinking.Using the Switch feels simple. You might start a game on the TV, then pull it out of the dock and keep playing from the couch or in bed without thinking much about it. Set it on a table, and the kickstand lets you prop it up for a quick match with a friend using the Joy-Cons separately. Those controllers are part of what makes it work so well. They attach to the sides when you want a handheld, or you can use them on their own without buying extras right away. Motion controls add another layer for games that support them (though not every title uses them well). And, as for its battery life, it ranges from about 4.5 to 9 hours, depending on the game, so lighter titles last longer, while more demanding ones will drain it faster.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
This is a refurbished unit with a Grade-A rating, so it should arrive close to brand new. Games aren't included, and storage is modest unless you add a microSD card, so you will need to budget for those separately. The original Switch obviously doesn't match the graphics or speed of the Switch 2, but the price is right, and you can still move between handheld, tabletop, and TV mode without changing setups, which makes it a practical choice for casual gaming, travel, or sharing quick sessions with friends.

        Nintendo announced the new The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time at its Nintendo Direct event this week. And already, Walmart has the game available for $59.99 (originally $69.99) for pre-order. Judging by how fast other pre-orders for the new remake have been going since the announcement, I wouldn't be surprised if this pre-order deal sells out too. And you're unlikely to see another discount on this major Nintendo game like the one Walmart is offering.
The Nintendo Switch 2 The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition console does not come with the game, so you will have to buy a physical or digital copy separately. Nintendo announced that the first printing of physical copies would include a "textured foil cover art" while supplies last, but it's unclear whether this sale is for that version. It would be inaccurate to call it a one-to-one remake. I'm hoping Nintendo finally gives us the Light Temple that the original game on the N64 could not fit in the game.             Credit: Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Microsoft Outlook is down for many users as of Monday afternoon.
                                            Downdetector highlights tens of thousands of users reports suggesting issues with Outlook.
                                            In addition, other Microsoft services, including Microsoft 365, are also down.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're trying to check your inbox or send an email in Microsoft Outlook, only to find the app uncooperative, you're not alone. Outlook is currently down for many users as of Monday afternoon. That's apparent to anyone who can't get the app to work: Downdetector, which highlights user reports for app outages, shows tens of thousands of reports as of 3:00 p.m. ET, and while the rate of reports does seem to be decreasing, thousands of reports keep coming in with every refresh.  As CNET reports, Microsoft has officially confirmed the outage itself. The company posted on its Microsoft 365 Status X account, stating: “We’ve identified an issue with an authentication component which is contributing to impact. To address this, we’ve developed a remediation strategy, and we’re applying it to a portion of infrastructure to test its efficacy. Once we’ve confirmed this resolves impact, we’ll apply the solution more broadly. For more information, please see EX1464935 in the admin center.”As such, the company should be rolling out a fix in due time, though it's difficult to say how long that may be. Recent outages have been fixed in a matter of hours, while others have stretched into the following day. At the time of writing, Downdetector shows that 38% of users are reporting issues receiving messages in Outlook, while 24% report issues with the app, and 21% with logging in. 
As it happens, Outlook isn't the only Microsoft product facing issues: Users report that Microsoft Teams, Microsoft Store, Microsoft Azur  and Microsoft 365 in general are experiencing  issues. In addition, OpenAI users are reporting issues with ChatGPT. 
            
                What do you think so far?

title: How to Disable ACR to Stop Your TV From Tracking You
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 8, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Proxima Studio/Shutterstock
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you have an LG TV, you might have woken up on Tuesday to some concerning headlines: A thorough investigation by YouTube channel Gamers Nexus found that LG TVs are capable of collecting an enormous amount of data, all without active participation from nearby users. Gamers Nexus showed that LG TVs can identify nearby devices and store their information, including things like device names, location, and IP addresses. The investigation argues that this might be why LG advertises itself as having access to 363 million "secondary" devices, despite posting only 216 million smart TV sales worldwide.    Most pressing of all, Gamers Nexus showed that LG TVs have the ability to record audio and save transcripts, even when the TV isn't actively connected to the internet. You might think you're preventing the worst of the tracking by disconnecting your TV from the network, but it's possible your conversations are being recorded all the same. To be clear, Gamers Nexus isn't saying that LG is purposely recording the conversations of every household that owns one of its TVs; the YouTube channel's point is that LG's TVs are capable of some serious data collection, and that their approach to user privacy is abysmal. Gamers Nexus includes interviews with LG executives who brag about how, because they "own" the hardware and software, they are able to learn a lot about the people in the vicinity of their TVs, and use that data for advertising.  While Gamers Nexus' findings are troubling, many aren't unique to LG. Smart TVs in general are not designed with user privacy in mind; in fact, they're often made to collect data specifically for advertising purposes. While there isn't much we can do about latent audio recording capabilities, there is something you can do to block a significant amount of data collection, no matter what smart TV you happen to own: Turn off ACR.  
How does your TV track what you watch?ACR, short for automatic content recognition, allows your smart TV to watch what you watch, identify what you watch, and use that information to recommend new content and serve you more relevant ads. Your TV observes moments in a show or movie (sometimes including audio) and will send that information to a database to match it against a library of content. ACR does this by literally taking screenshots of what is happening on your screen, roughly two per second. That enables tracking on everything, whether you use your smart TV apps, a Blu-ray player, a device like an Apple TV, or a PlayStation—whatever you display on your TV, ACR can watch and report. Most major TV manufacturers put ACR tracking in their devices. After Vizio got into hot water years ago for not properly disclosing how much data they were stealing from customers, TV manufacturers started baking these settings into initial setup agreements. If you’re like me, you accidentally agreed to this tracking without realizing it, because you were too focused on getting your TV set up to care about, you know, reading a legal document.If you have a smart TV, it likely has ACR tracking you can disable. However, all TV manufacturers call this option something different. I'll run through some of the top brands, what they each call their ACR settings, and where to find them. Even still, these brands change their settings menus and settings names all the time, so even if you have a TV from a company listed here, you might not find my instructions relevant. Your best bet, if these instructions don't help, is to Google your specific TV model and where to find its ACR settings. You should be able to find a guide from the manufacturer or a walkthrough from someone with access to your TV who knows where to find the setting. But if you have an LG, Samsung, Sony, Hisense, or TCL, follow along below: 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
LG TVsIf you have an LG smart TV (like me), then your ACR settings are going to be under Live Plus. The setting sounds innocent enough, but it’s likely meant to so that you keep it enabled. You’ll find this option in Settings > General > System > Additional (or Advanced) Settings > Live Plus. While you’re here, you might as well enable “Limit Ad Tracking” under Advertisement.Samsung TVsLet’s take a look at another popular TV brand, Samsung. On newer models, head to Settings > All Settings > General & Privacy > Terms & Privacy. Then, turn off Viewing Information Services and Interest-Based Advertising. On older models, you’ll find your ACR options in the sidebar menu under Privacy Choices > Terms & Conditions, Privacy Policy. Just make sure to disable “Viewing Information Services."Sony TVsSony keeps their ACR options under Settings > Initial Setup > Samba Interactive TV. From here, disable Samba Interactive TV. In addition, you might find ad tracking features under About > Ads > Ads Personalization.Hisense TVsHisense keeps its ACR under Settings > System > Privacy. Its name will depend on your particular model, but it might be called "Smart TV Experience" or "Viewing Information Services." TCL keeps its settings under Settings > Privacy > Smart TV Experience. Here, disable "Use Info from TV Inputs."Amazon Fire TVAmazon TVs don't seem to hide ACR settings that much. On these TVs, you'll find these options under Preferences > Privacy Settings. Here, turn off Automatic Content Recognition.

title: 10 Hacks Every Proton Mail User Should Know
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 4, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Zain bin Awais/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Proton Mail is a privacy-focused mail service that strips trackers from messages, maintains zero-access encryption (meaning Proton can't read or hand over the content of your emails), and offers end-to-end encryption between Proton mailboxes. If you're a Proton user, there are a handful of other hacks you should know to maximize these privacy features and make sending and receiving emails as seamless as possible. Proton Mail is free to use if you have just one email address, but storage is limited to just 500 MB, which will fill up fast if you are receiving messages with large attachments. You can upgrade to a Plus subscription for $4 per month to get 15 GB of storage—the same amount available to most Google users—but if you don't want to pay anything, you can at least double your limit to 1 GB by completing Proton's onboarding process within 18 days of signing up. Look for a Get more storage option on the left sidebar of your mailbox, and click an action to complete the task. Once you've finished the checklist, you'll unlock an additional 500 MB of storage on your account. Reserve an email address for your child in their nameIf you have a relatively common name, it's likely that many email addresses using simple conventions, such as firstname.lastname, have already been claimed. By the time your kids are old enough to set up their own accounts, pickings may be even slimmer. You can go ahead and reserve a username through Proton Mail for them, and they have 15 years to activate it. Once they're old enough, they'll already have a private email set up. Choose an address and pay $1 toward the Proton Foundation, then save the voucher to share with your child down the line. 
Use Easy Switch to migrate external email addressesIf you're moving to Proton Mail from a different email provider or simply want all of your messages in one inbox, you can use Proton's Easy Switch feature to connect with and import from Gmail, Yahoo Mail, Outlook, and any other provider that allows IMAP access. Once Easy Switch is on, you'll be able to receive and send messages from your external address within Proton, and any mail sent to another Proton user from that address will be end-to-end encrypted. You'll retain copies of messages in your external inbox, so you don't need to make the full transition immediately. Easy Switch can also migrate your contacts and calendars. Go to Settings > Import via Easy Switch, choose your email service, and follow the prompts. Customize the Undo Send timer to recall emailsWe've all sent emails we wish we could take back thanks to a typo we didn't notice, an attachment we forgot to add, or a message we regret. Proton Mail has a delayed send feature that gives you up to 20 seconds to change your mind before your email is out of your hands. The timer is set at 10 seconds by default, but you can adjust it down to 0 or 5 seconds or up to 20. Go to Settings > Messages and composing, scroll down to the Composing section, and choose your desired time from the Undo send dropdown.Create aliases to filter mail to specific foldersThere are plenty of good reasons to use an email alias, from keeping your primary address private to easily filtering messages from mailing lists. Proton Mail supports unlimited plus addressing, meaning you can simply add a plus symbol and word after your username to create a new email—such as [username][email protected]—and receive messages in your regular inbox (with filters if you set them up). This can be done when you sign up for an account or add your email to a list. Alternatively, you can create a randomly generated email alias, which keeps your username hidden. Free users get up to 10, while paid subscribers can create unlimited aliases. On the web interface, click the security shield icon, go to Hide-my-email aliases, and click New alias. Add a password to encrypt emails to non-Proton usersMessages between Proton users are automatically encrypted end to end, but if your recipient doesn't use Proton Mail, you can set up a password for your emails to keep them private. Replies to password-protected emails are also encrypted (though your reply to that reply will require you to re-enable encryption). When you compose your message, click the padlock icon in the bottom toolbar and enter a password and password hint. You can set an expiration date as well. Note that you'll need to share the password with the recipient separately.  
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Set expiration timers to automatically delete emails from recipients’ inboxesAnother Proton Mail security feature is the expiration timer, which will auto-delete emails you send and receive after a set period, preventing messages from hanging around in inboxes and sent folders indefinitely. Messages that you send to other Proton Mail users as well as password-protected emails to those outside of Proton can be set to expire. If you have a paid account, you can also set emails you receive to self-destruct (in addition to auto-delete for messages in trash). Click the hourglass icon at the bottom of the message and set the expiration date and time. If you are sending a password-protected email to a non-Proton user, check the box. Then hit Set. When you take a photo, image metadata may reveal locations, times and dates, and other information that can be used to track you if it falls into the wrong hands. Proton Mail can strip that out for sent images, so you can share photos via email without giving any unnecessary data away. When you attach an image to an email draft, choose Remove metadata when prompted. Turn on Message Content Search to build a local and searchable index of your emails Because of Proton's encryption, the standard search feature reads only names, dates, email addresses, and subject lines. If you want to include message content, you'll need to enable the feature that builds a local index in your browser, protecting it from intrusion unless someone has physical access to your device. Click the search bar at the top of your inbox on the web app and tap Enable next to Search message content. Click Enable to confirm. Note that indexing does require storage space, but once complete, it'll automatically update as long as your browser is open. Activate your short domain to get a shorter, simpler addressBy default, Proton Mail addresses end in @proton.me (unless you connect your own domain). But users on paid plans have the option to add a short domain, which is simply [username]@pm.me. You can send messages from either, and both route to your inbox. The shorter address is easier to remember and share, such as when you're giving our your email over the phone. To enable it, go to Settings > Identity and addresses. You must be a paid subscriber to activate a short domain address—if you downgrade to the free plan, you will still be able to receive (but not send) messages sent to your @pm.me address.

schema.headline: 10 Hacks Every Proton Mail User Should Know
